newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha goes north to drum up support.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha goes north to drum up support.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha took his cross-country campaign to shore up flagging popular support to this northern city on Saturday amid threats of renewed opposition protests in the capital Tirana.

A crowd of about 300, most of them children and students, had converged in the morning sun outside Shkoder's sports hall where Berisha was expected to address a carefully selected group of party faithfuls.
Police kept a low profile and many of the town's residents appeared unimpressed by their president's visit as they went about their routine morning errands.

"The meeting is by invitation only, which shows that he doesn't trust us," said an elderly man selling rice and vegetables from his little make-shift stand at the town's dusty main market. "Everything will be well controlled."

Faced with massive popular unrest sparked by the collapse of dubious investment schemes that cost many Albanians their life savings, the embattled president has criss-crossed the nation over the past week to promise his people that the right-wing government will do what it can to ease their plight.

He has made a series of impassioned speeches to groups of hand-picked supporters in the capital Tirana and three regional towns, vowing to speed up economic growth and promising to exempt some destitute investors from paying taxes for two years.
In Tirana, opposition parties said on Saturday they had been denied permission to stage a mid-day rally in a central soccer stadium, but said the meeting may go ahead anyway.

"The interior ministry told us we can't hold a rally in the stadium because there was a soccer match underway. So I guess people will just go and see the match -- I myself am a big soccer fan," senior socialist leader Namik Dokle told Reuters.

Soccer matches have been banned in Albania since last month because of fears that large gatherings of spectators could spark anti-government protests and officials said national league games were not scheduled to resume before next week.

The opposition blames Berisha and the Democratic Party government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi for not having reined in the investment schemes which blossomed in Albania after the fall of its hardline Stalinist regime in 1990.

Violence broke out in Tirana on Thursday when a group of opposition supporters, trying to reach central Skanderbeg Square after a peaceful rally in the suburbs, clashed with riot police and scores of plain-clothes security forces.

Protesters hurled stones at police, who threw stones back and fired into the air to disperse the angry crowd. Several demonstrators were injured and authorities said five policemen were slightly hurt.

The government, faced with the biggest crisis in its five-year rule, blames the unrest on left-wing extremists linked to Albania's Stalinist past, who it says are bent on destabilising the Balkan nation.

Berisha's campaign appears to have had little effect on thousands of enraged protesters in the country's south, who have staged weeks of mass demonstrations to demand the government reimburse them for their losses and then resign.

In the Adriatic port town of Vlore, some 7,000 marchers turned out for the 18th successive day while a group of 60 students continued a hunger strike for a third day to demand the government's resignation.
Berisha has said he will travel to Vlore, where three protesters died during pitched street battles with police last week, but no date has yet been announced for his visit.
